neighbours.label: use-it-or-lose-it contexts: text about a body part, mind or skill that goes unused or inactive, at the point where the resulting decay (atrophy, stagnation, stiffness) is about to be named or prevented; not other harms or other 'prevent'/'bad for'
fire: Astronauts on long missions lift weights daily to keep their bones from thinning.
A joint that is kept in a cast for weeks will become stiff and weak.
Retired people who stop solving problems often find their memory fading.
Stretch your fingers every hour to prevent the tendons from tightening up.
Lying in bed for a month is terrible for your leg muscles.
A talent that is never practised will slowly wither.
Elderly residents are encouraged to walk each day to avoid losing their strength.
When you stop speaking a language, your vocabulary begins to shrink.
quiet: Astronauts on long missions wear dosimeters daily to keep track of their radiation.
A joint that is hit by a hammer will become swollen and sore.
Retired people who start a business often find their savings shrinking.
Wash your hands every hour to prevent the virus from spreading around.
Smoking a pack a day is terrible for your lungs.
A debt that is never repaid will slowly grow.
Elderly residents are encouraged to lock the door each day to avoid losing their valuables.
When you start heating a metal, its length begins to increase.

notes: Card: 'a brain that is not learning becomes stagnant', 'exercise to avoid muscle atrophy', 'staying still is bad for your spine'; output promotes idle, bored, atrophy, unused, stagnant. Probes: disuse sentences 0.47-0.94; 'helmet to prevent head injuries' 0.07, 'not insured' 0.03, 'sugar is bad for your teeth' 0.04. Near misses keep prevent / bad for / not + participle with a different kind of harm.
